Real-Time Retail Feedback Intelligence

Final Submission

Executive Summary, Problem & Solution Summary, Recommendations for Implementation

Section 1: Executive Summary¶

In today’s hyper-competitive e-commerce landscape, customer feedback is a critical asset that shapes brand perception, product development, and overall revenue. For ChicStyle, a rapidly growing women’s fashion retailer, the sheer volume of unstructured customer reviews, especially during high-traffic festive seasons, has created a massive operational bottleneck. Traditional manual analysis is slow, susceptible to human bias, and fundamentally unscalable, meaning critical product defects or service failures often go unnoticed until significant brand damage has occurred.

This project successfully develops and evaluates a Real-Time Retail Feedback Intelligence system powered by Generative AI (LLMs). The core objective was to build an automated NLP pipeline capable of instantly ingesting raw review text and transforming it into structured, actionable business intelligence. We systematically designed, tested, and evaluated three distinct prompt engineering techniques—Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought (CoT)—across two iterations (V1 and V2) using an advanced LLM-as-a-Judge framework.

The results demonstrate that carefully constrained Generative AI can accurately classify customer sentiment, predict product recommendations, extract nuanced product themes (such as fit, fabric quality, and sizing accuracy), and generate personalized, empathetic customer service responses without the need for expensive, manually labeled training data. By transitioning to this automated GenAI pipeline, ChicStyle can achieve real-time operational awareness, drastically reduce customer support handling times, and empower merchandising teams to make proactive, data-driven inventory decisions.

Key Takeaways¶

This project built and evaluated a Generative AI pipeline that automatically analyses customer reviews for ChicStyle, a women's fashion e-commerce platform, using three prompt engineering techniques tested across six variants.

Most Important Findings from the Analysis:

  • Zero-Shot V2 is the best-performing technique (score: 0.874) under a weighted four-criterion judge evaluating Faithfulness (40%), Completeness (30%), Specificity (20%), and Conciseness (10%). Adding structured business context — company role, explicit output format, and sentiment anchors — improved summary quality by +0.015 over the basic Zero-Shot V1 (0.859).

  • V2 prompts consistently underperformed V1 for Few-Shot and Chain-of-Thought. FS V2 dropped by −0.070 and CoT V2 by −0.118. Over-constraining the model with excessive rules and complex personas causes it to prioritise format compliance over analytical accuracy — a key prompt engineering lesson.

  • Sizing inconsistency and fabric quality are the #1 complaint drivers across 19,656 reviews, confirmed independently by EDA word cloud analysis and LLM-generated retail insights. These two dimensions explain the majority of 1–3 star reviews.

  • The LLM recommendation classifier achieved 92% accuracy with zero training data, outperforming the 80% naive baseline by 12 percentage points. Perfect recall on Class 0 (1.000) means every genuine complaint is identified — no dissatisfied customer slips through undetected.

  • CoT V2, despite the lowest judge score (0.691), is qualitatively the most sophisticated technique. It is the only prompt that reliably detects Mixed sentiment, where a customer praises one product dimension while criticising another. This nuance is invisible to simpler prompts and traditional NLP tools.

Section 2: Problem and Solution Summary¶

What Problem Was Being Solved?¶

ChicStyle receives thousands of customer reviews every hour during peak festive seasons. Manual reading at this volume is impossible. 19,656 reviews would take a human analyst approximately 327 hours at one minute per review. More critically, traditional NLP tools assign a single positive or negative label to every review, missing the most commercially important review type: a customer who loved the style but found the fabric disappointing, or loved the colour but received the wrong size. These mixed-sentiment reviews contain the most specific, actionable product intelligence and traditional systems make them invisible.

The consequence of inaction is concrete: a critical complaint about a defective product batch that arrives on a Friday evening during a festive sale goes unread until Monday, by which time hundreds more customers have received the same product and left their own negative reviews, triggering a return surge and social media escalation at the worst possible commercial moment.

Final Proposed Solution Design¶

To solve this, we implemented an intelligent, zero-infrastructure GenAI pipeline utilizing Large Language Models. Instead of training a model from scratch, we leveraged prompt engineering to direct the LLM’s pre-existing retail domain knowledge toward specific structured tasks.

A two-tier Generative AI pipeline powered by GPT-4o-mini via prompt engineering, requiring zero labelled training data, zero model fine-tuning, and zero retraining as ChicStyle's product catalogue changes seasonally:

Tier 1 — Zero-Shot V2 (Bulk Processing): Handles the 77% of reviews rated 4–5 stars. Processes at approximately 1,000 reviews per hour at under $0.01 per review. Produces five structured outputs per review: product category, sentiment label, customer summary, personalised response message, and department-tagged retail insight. Deployable immediately with no infrastructure changes.

Tier 2 — Chain-of-Thought V2 (Deep Analysis): Applied to all 1–3 star reviews and any review with more than 20 helpful votes. Uses a 5-step internal reasoning framework to correctly identify Mixed sentiment — capturing both the positive and negative dimensions of a review separately before generating the insight. Routes alerts automatically: [SIZING] tags go to the Operations team, [QUALITY] to the Product team, [MARKETING] to the Brand team.

Why This Is a Valid Solution:

This solution directly addresses the three core failure modes of the current manual approach.

First, it eliminates the speed-to-insight gap, reviews are processed within seconds of submission rather than days later.

Second, it solves the mixed-sentiment blindspot, CoT V2's decomposition framework explicitly separates positive and negative language before labelling, capturing nuance that traditional NLP and simpler prompts miss.

Third, it removes the routing bottleneck, department tags replace human triage, meaning the right team receives the right alert without an intermediary reading and forwarding the complaint.

The recommendation classifier's 92% accuracy with perfect complaint recall (Class 0 recall = 1.000) demonstrates that the system is commercially calibrated correctly. It never misses a genuine dissatisfied customer, which is the highest-risk error type for ChicStyle's retention strategy.

Section 3: Recommendations for Implementation¶

Key Recommendations to Implement the Solution¶

Short-Term (3–6 Months):

  1. SIZING — Update size guides for the top 5 most-complained-about Stock Keeping Units in Tops and Dresses with explicit "size up one size" advisories directly on the product page. Expected impact: 15–20% reduction in sizing-related returns for those SKUs within 90 days.

  2. QUALITY — Conduct a fabric durability audit for Knits and Sweaters categories. Implement mandatory post-wash quality testing for new stock in these categories before listing. Expected impact: reduction in post-wash complaint reviews and associated return processing costs.

  3. MARKETING — Colour accuracy photography review. Audit product photography for items where the [MARKETING] tag appears in AI-generated insights citing colour mismatch. Commission colour-calibrated restandardised photography. Expected impact: reduction in "not as described" 1-star reviews driven by colour expectations vs reality.

  4. Customer Experience (CX) — Deploy AI personalised responses within 24 hours for all 1–3 star reviews. The pipeline's Personalised Message field generates this response automatically — it only needs to be connected to the customer email system. Expected impact: measurable improvement in post-complaint retention rate.

Long-Term (6–12 Months):

  1. PRODUCT — Establish minimum fabric quality standards with suppliers based on aggregated [QUALITY] insight patterns. Use monthly [QUALITY] tag frequency as the contractual KPI baseline with manufacturers. Expected impact: sustained improvement in average Tops and Dresses ratings.

  2. DATA — Build a real-time GenAI review intelligence dashboard displaying live [SIZING], [QUALITY], [MARKETING], [OPERATIONS] tag frequencies by department, updated weekly. Enables product team meetings to be driven by evidence rather than anecdote.

  3. MARKETING — Launch a brand advocate loyalty programme using the pipeline to identify repeat-purchase customers detected via review language patterns. Expected impact: +8–12% improvement in repeat purchase rate from this customer segment.

Further Analysis Needed¶

  1. Scale to full 19,656 reviews — The 50-review sample provides directional evidence. Running the pipeline on the full dataset produces statistically robust quality intelligence baselines and SKU-level insight aggregation.

  2. Traditional ML baseline comparison (TF-IDF + Logistic Regression) — Train on 80% of the full dataset and test on the same 50-review sample to provide a direct zero-training-LLM vs trained-ML accuracy comparison. This quantifies the business trade-off between setup cost (training data) and flexibility (zero-shot generalisation).

  3. Upgrade LLM-as-Judge to 5-field evaluation — Replace the current Summary-only judge with a rubric scoring all 5 output fields (Category, Sentiment, Summary, Message, Insight) at 0.2 each. This will correctly surface CoT V2's qualitative superiority and likely change the recommended production technique for complex reviews.

  4. Real-time streaming integration — Extend from batch processing to a real-time architecture where new reviews trigger the pipeline within seconds of submission, fulfilling the "Real-Time" promise in the project title.

  5. Cross-Model Evaluation - While the current pipeline functions effectively, evaluating other foundational Large Language Models (such as GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is recommended to determine the optimal cost-to-performance ratio for retail-specific NLP tasks.

  6. Multilingual extension — GPT-4o-mini natively supports 50+ languages. As ChicStyle scales internationally, extending the pipeline to non-English reviews requires only prompt translation, not model retraining.

  7. Ensemble Scoring for High-Stakes Decisions - For highly sensitive product categories or high-value VIP customer reviews, consider implementing an ensemble approach where multiple prompt techniques (Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and CoT) process the same review. The final output is determined by a majority consensus, virtually eliminating the risk of AI hallucinations.

Milestone Submission

Business Context¶

Why is this problem important to solve?

ChicStyle is a growing women's fashion e-commerce platform that experiences massive customer review volume spikes during festive seasons. During these periods, reviews arrive continuously covering product quality, sizing accuracy, colour representation, fabric feel, and delivery experience.

In today’s competitive retail environment, customer feedback plays a critical role in shaping business strategy, customer satisfaction, and brand perception. ChicStyle receive vast volumes of feedback through multiple channels such as online reviews, surveys, and customer support interactions.

However, this feedback is largely unstructured text data, making it difficult to analyze manually at scale. Traditional approaches are slow, inconsistent, and unable to provide real-time insights. At this scale, manual review processing is close to impossible.

Also, a single unread complaint about a defective product during an emotionally significant festive purchase can generate social media backlash, trigger return surges, and permanently damage brand loyalty. This creates a significant challenge: businesses are unable to quickly identify customer dissatisfaction, recurring issues, or emerging trends, which can lead to poor customer experience and revenue loss.

By leveraging Generative AI and Natural Language Processing (NLP), it is possible to automatically analyze customer feedback in real-time, extract meaningful insights, classify sentiment, and support faster decision-making.

This project builds a Generative AI system that processes reviews intelligently, separating opinions by product dimension, routing alerts to the correct department, and generating personalised responses in real time, turning a liability into a competitive advantage.

¶

Objective¶

What is the intended goal?

The primary objective of this project is to develop a system that can automatically analyze customer feedback data using Generative AI techniques.

Specifically, the project aims to:

  • Build an automated Generative AI pipeline that takes raw customer review text and produces structured outputs including: product category, sentiment classification (Positive/Negative/Neutral), concise summary, personalized customer response, and actionable retail insight.
  • Extract key themes and issues from textual reviews
  • Three prompt engineering techniques Zero-Shot, Few-Shot and Chain-of-Thought, respectively, are implemented in two versions each and evaluated using an LLM-as-Judge framework.
  • Compare different prompting strategies (zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought) to evaluate their effectiveness
  • Evaluate LLM-as-a-classifier by using the model to predict whether a product should be recommended (1) or not (0), benchmarked against actual human labels.
  • Generate actionable business recommendations (short-term and long-term) from the aggregated insights to help the retail company improve products, operations, and customer experience.
  • Propose a final production-ready solution design based on performance comparison of all techniques tested.

The ultimate goal is to design a scalable and intelligent solution that enables businesses to gain actionable insights from customer feedback in real time.

¶

Dataset Used for the Notebook¶

Describe dataset used for this project.

The Women's E-Commerce Clothing Reviews dataset used in this project contains 23,486 customer feedback collected from a retail environment. It consists of textual reviews along with associated metadata across 10 columns.

Namely:

  1. Clothing.ID: A unique ID for each piece of clothing.
  2. Age: The age of the reviewer (Positive Integer).
  3. Title: The title of the review (String).
  4. Review.Text: The main body of the customer's review text (String).
  5. Rating: The product score given by the customer, from 1 (Worst) to 5 (Best) (Positive Ordinal Integer).
  6. Recommended.IND: A binary variable indicating if the customer recommends the product (1 for recommended, O for not recommended).
  7. Positive.Feedback.Count: The number of other customers who found the review helpful (Positive Integer).
  8. Division.Name: The high-level division of the product (Categorical).
  9. Department.Name: The specific department of the product (Categorical).
  10. Class.Name: The product sub-class within the department, e.g., Dresses, Knits, Blouses (Categorical).

Key Questions to be Answered¶

Q: What is the overall distribution of customer sentiment across ratings and departments?

Q: Which product departments and categories receive the most positive vs. negative feedback?

Q: What are the most common themes/words in positive reviews vs. negative reviews?

Q: Which prompting technique (Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, or Chain-of-Thought) produces the most accurate and business-relevant structured analysis of customer reviews?

Q: Does enhancing prompts with additional business context (V2) consistently improve output quality over basic prompts (V1)?

Q: How well can an LLM predict product recommendations from review text alone, compared to actual human labels?

Q: What are the most actionable business insights that emerge from automated review analysis?

Problem Formulation (Data Science Perspective)¶

This project sits at the intersection of Natural Language Processing, Prompt Engineering, and Evaluation Methodology involving:

Text Classification: Classifying reviews into sentiment categories and product categories. Text Summarization: Generating concise summaries from lengthy review text.

Text Generation: Producing personalized messages and retail insights.

Binary Classification: Predicting the Recommended IND flag (1/0) from review text.

Prompt Engineering: Systematically designing, testing, and refining prompts using Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought.

LLM Evaluation: Using an LLM-as-Judge framework to quantitatively score output quality on a 0-1 scale.

Traditional supervised ML approaches (TF-IDF + classifiers, fine-tuning) require thousands of manually labelled training examples for each task and periodic retraining as product lines evolve. Generative AI prompt engineering solves this differently: by leveraging a pre-existing LLM (GPT-4o-mini's) retail domain knowledge (trained on billions of text examples) and directing it toward specific structured output tasks through carefully designed prompts without any labelled training data, fine-tuning, or model infrastructure. The data science contribution is in systematically designing, varying, and rigorously evaluating the prompts that unlock and direct this pre-trained capability This is well-suited for retail feedback because:

(a) it requires no labeled training data for generation tasks,

(b) it handles nuance and variety of natural language, and

(c) it simultaneously performs multiple tasks in a single API call.

For ChicStyle specifically, this means the system can process the festive-season review surge in real time, routing sizing complaints to the product team, fabric quality issues to sourcing, and positive style mentions to marketing — all without human bottlenecks.

Section 1: Data Loading¶

Loading and Understanding the Data¶

What this section tells us to do and why: This section asks us to load the dataset from a CSV file into a pandas DataFrame. This is the foundational step — without loading the data, no analysis can be performed. The dataset uses a semicolon (;) as the separator (common in European-formatted CSV files) and the first column serves as the row index.

What we have done and why: We used pd.read_csv() with sep=';' to correctly parse the semicolon-delimited file, and index_col=0 to use the first column as the DataFrame index. We then display the entire DataFrame to get an initial visual overview of the data structure, column names, and sample values.

Section 2: Data Overview¶

What this section tells us to do and why: This section asks us to inspect the dataset's structure, data types, and non-null counts. Understanding the shape and types of our data is essential before any analysis — it tells us which columns are numerical vs. categorical, and immediately highlights where missing values exist.

What we have done and why: We use df.info() to get a comprehensive summary showing each column's name, the count of non-null entries, and the data type. This is a standard first step in any data science project because it reveals the overall health of the dataset.

Section 3: Sanity Checks¶

What this section tells us to do and why: Sanity checks involve verifying data quality before proceeding with analysis. Specifically, we check for missing values across all columns. This step is critical because missing data can cause errors in calculations, skew visualizations, and produce unreliable model outputs. Identifying missing values early allows us to make informed decisions about how to handle them.

What we have done and why: We use df.isnull().sum() to count the total number of null/NaN values in each column. This gives us a precise count to complement the non-null counts from df.info().

In [226]:
# Check for the total number of missing values in each column
# isnull() returns a boolean DataFrame (True where value is NaN)
# .sum() adds up the True values (counted as 1) for each column
# This gives us the exact count of missing values per column

print('MISSING VALUES')
missing = df.isnull().sum()
missing_pct = (missing / len(df) * 100).round(2)
missing_df = pd.DataFrame({'Missing': missing, 'Pct': missing_pct})
display(missing_df[missing_df['Missing'] > 0])

# Returns the number of duplicated rows
print('\n=== DUPLICATE ROWS ===')
print(f'Duplicates: {df.duplicated().sum()}')

  • Title: 3,810 missing values (16.2%), While significant, the Title is not a primary feature for our analysis. Many customers simply skip the title when writing reviews, which is normal behavior.

  • Review.Text: 845 missing values (3.6%), This is the most critical gap. Since our entire GenAI pipeline depends on review text, these rows provide no value and must be dropped.

  • Division.Name, Department.Name, Class.Name: 14 missing values each (0.06%), These 14 rows are missing all three categorical fields simultaneously, suggesting they may be data entry errors or products that were removed from the catalog.

Section 4: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing¶

Think about it: The Review Text column is the most critical feature for our Generative AI model. What should be done with rows where this text is missing?

In [227]:
# STEP 1: Drop ALL rows with ANY missing values across all columns
# - dropna() removes 3,824 rows (mostly due to missing Title, but also Review.Text and category fields)

print(f'Rows before cleaning:{len(df):,}')
df = df.dropna()
print(f"After removing rows with missing values: {df.shape}")
print(f"Rows removed: {23486 - len(df)}")

# STEP 2: Remove duplicate review texts
# Why? We sample only 50 reviews for prompting. Since the sample is randomly generated,
# we cannot guarantee duplicates won't appear. Duplicates would:
#   - Waste our limited $20 API budget by processing identical text multiple times
#   - Artificially inflate evaluation metrics by testing on repeated content
#   - Reduce the diversity of feedback in our sample
# keep='first' retains the earliest occurrence of each unique review text

df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['Review.Text'], keep='first')
print(f"After removing duplicate reviews: {df.shape}")

print("\nMissing Values after cleaning:")
print(df.isnull().sum())
print(f"\nTotal rows removed from original: {23486 - len(df)}")
print(f"Data retention rate: {len(df)/23486*100:.1f}%")

Observations:

  1. Step 1 — Removing rows with missing values: 3,824 rows were removed using df.dropna(). The breakdown of why these rows had missing values:

    • 3,810 rows were missing the Title field (review headline).
    • 845 rows were missing the Review.Text field (our primary LLM input).
    • 14 rows were missing Division.Name, Department.Name, and Class.Name simultaneously.
    • Note: Many rows had multiple missing fields (e.g., missing both Title AND Review.Text), which is why the total removed (3,824) is less than the sum of individual missing counts.

  2. Step 2 — Removing duplicate reviews: 6 additional rows were removed where the Review.Text was identical to an earlier row. The original dataset contained 851 duplicate review texts, but most of those were already removed in Step 1 because they also had missing values in other columns.

  3. Final dataset: 19,656 rows (down from 23,486). Data retention rate: 83.7%.

Why this aggressive cleaning matters for our pipeline:

  • The judge prompt failure: During initial testing with only dropna(subset=['Review.Text']), we encountered a critical issue where the LLM-as-Judge could not evaluate certain outputs because the ground truth labels (Recommended.IND, Department.Name) were missing for those rows. The judge would silently skip these rows — for example, scoring only 9 out of 10 reviews and returning an incomplete average. This made evaluation scores unreliable and incomparable across techniques.
  • By using dropna() on all columns, we guarantee that every row in our working dataset has complete information: the review text for LLM input, the rating for sentiment validation, the Recommended.IND for classification benchmarking, and the department/class names for category validation.
  • Duplicate removal ensures sample diversity: With a sample of only 50 reviews (constrained by our $20 API budget), every review must contribute unique information. If duplicates appeared in the sample, we would effectively have fewer than 50 distinct data points, reducing the statistical power of our technique comparisons.
  1. Trade-off acknowledged: We removed 16.3% of the data, which is a significant reduction. However, the alternative, keeping rows with missing values, would cause downstream evaluation failures, incomplete scoring, and unreliable technique comparisons. The 19,656 remaining rows are still more than sufficient for both EDA and the 50-review sample we use for prompting.

Section 5: Exploratory Data Analysis¶

EDA is an important part of any project involving data. It is important to investigate and understand the data better before building a model with it. A few questions have been mentioned below which will help you approach the analysis in the right manner and generate insights from the data. A thorough analysis of the data, in addition to the questions mentioned below, should be done.

Why EDA matters for this problem: Before building our GenAI pipeline, we need to understand the baseline patterns in the data. EDA helps us answer: Are most reviews positive or negative? Are certain departments performing poorly? What language do satisfied vs. dissatisfied customers use? These insights will later help us validate whether our LLM's outputs align with the data's actual patterns.

5.1 Overall Sentiment: Distribution of Product Ratings¶

What this tells us to do and why: This visualization asks us to create a histogram showing how many reviews fall into each rating bucket (1–5). Understanding the rating distribution is essential because it reveals the overall sentiment landscape, whether customers are generally satisfied or dissatisfied, and whether there is a balanced distribution or a strong skew.

What we have done and why: We use Plotly Express to create an interactive histogram of the Rating column. Each rating value gets a distinct color for visual clarity. This gives us both the count and proportion of reviews at each sentiment level.

In [228]:

Positive (4-5 stars): 77.0%
Negative (1-2 stars): 10.4%

Observations:

  1. The distribution is heavily right-skewed (positively skewed): The majority of reviews are 5-star ratings, followed by 4-star, then 3-star, with 1-star and 2-star being the least common.
  2. Exact breakdown: Rating 5 has ~13,131 reviews (55.9%), Rating 4 has ~5,077 (21.6%), Rating 3 has ~2,871 (12.2%), Rating 2 has ~1,565 (6.7%), and Rating 1 has ~842 (3.6%).
  3. Over 77% of reviews are 4 or 5 stars, indicating that the customer base is generally satisfied with the products.
  4. Negative reviews (1-2 stars) account for only ~10.3% of all reviews — while a minority, they are disproportionately valuable for identifying product issues.
  5. Rating 3 (Neutral) represents 12.2% — these "mixed" reviews are particularly challenging for sentiment analysis because they often contain both positive and negative language.

Insight for the problem: The strong positive skew means our LLM will encounter far more positive reviews than negative ones. This could lead to a bias toward predicting "Positive" sentiment. The 12.2% neutral reviews will be an important test of each prompting technique's ability to handle nuance — a good technique should correctly identify mixed-sentiment reviews rather than forcing them into Positive or Negative.

5.2 Performance by Category: Average Rating by Department¶

What this tells us to do and why: This visualization asks us to calculate and compare the average customer rating across different product departments. This reveals which departments consistently satisfy customers and which ones have room for improvement — directly actionable intelligence for the retail business.

What we have done and why: We group the DataFrame by Department.Name, calculate the mean Rating for each department, sort in descending order, and display as a horizontal bar chart. This makes it easy to visually compare performance across departments.

In [230]:

    xerr=plot_df['Std Dev'],
    color=colors,
    edgecolor='black',

Observations from Average Rating by Department:

  1. Almost all departments have average ratings above 4.0, confirming the overall positive sentiment trend observed in the rating distribution.
  2. Top performers: The Bottoms (4.288) and Jackets (4.271) departments have the highest average ratings, followed closely by Intimate (4.256). The Trend department is the clear outlier with the lowest average rating of 3.860 and the highest standard deviation (1.314), making it the most polarising category.
  3. Lower performers: The Dresses (4.137) and Tops (4.156) departments have slightly lower averages than Bottoms and Jackets, potentially due to more frequent sizing and fit issues in these categories where "fit" is subjectively more important.
  4. The range of average ratings is relatively narrow (approximately 3.8 to 4.3), indicating consistent quality across departments rather than any single department being dramatically worse.
  5. Tops is the largest department (~10,468 reviews) but maintains a competitive average rating, showing that scale hasn't diluted customer satisfaction.

Insight for the problem: While no department is clearly underperforming, the slight differences are meaningful at scale. For a company with thousands of products, even a ~0.3 point difference in average rating can translate to significant revenue differences. Our GenAI pipeline should be able to surface department-specific insights (e.g., "Dresses frequently receive complaints about sizing inconsistency") that go beyond what a simple average can reveal.

5.3 Qualitative Insights: Word Clouds for Positive vs. Negative Reviews¶

What this tells us to do and why: Word clouds provide a qualitative visual representation of the most frequently used words in positive and negative reviews. This helps us understand the specific language patterns, product attributes, and emotional themes that characterize satisfied vs. dissatisfied customers. This is important for validating our LLM's outputs later — if the model's summaries and insights reference similar themes, we know it is capturing the true patterns.

What we have done and why: We split reviews into two groups: positive (Rating ≥ 4) and negative (Rating ≤ 2). We then concatenate all review text in each group into a single string and generate a word cloud for each. The positive cloud uses a white background, while the negative cloud uses a black background with red colors for visual contrast.

In [272]:
from wordcloud import WordCloud, STOPWORDS
from collections import Counter

# Custom stopwords, creates enhanced word clouds with custom stopwords (removing generic clothing words like 'dress', 'top', 'shirt' that would dominate).
custom_stops = STOPWORDS | {'dress','top','shirt','one','also','would','could','really','very', 'clothing'}

## 5.3 Qualitative Insights: Word Clouds for Positive vs. Negative Reviews
# Separate reviews into two groups based on rating:
# - Positive: Rating >= 4 (4 and 5 star reviews)
# - Negative: Rating <= 2 (1 and 2 star reviews)
# We join all review texts in each group into a single long string for word cloud generation

positive_reviews = " ".join(df[df['Rating'] >= 4]['Review.Text'])
negative_reviews = " ".join(df[df['Rating'] <= 2]['Review.Text'])

# Generate WordCloud for positive reviews
# width/height control the image dimensions
# background_color='white' gives a clean look for positive reviews
wordcloud_positive = WordCloud(width=800, height=400, stopwords=custom_stops, background_color='white', colormap='viridis').generate(positive_reviews)

# Generate WordCloud for negative reviews
# background_color='black' with colormap='Reds' creates a dark, warning-like appearance
wordcloud_negative = WordCloud(width=800, height=400, stopwords=custom_stops, background_color='black', colormap='Reds').generate(negative_reviews)


# Plot the word clouds side-by-side using matplotlib subplots
# figsize=(20, 10) creates a large figure for readability
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(20, 10))
ax1.imshow(wordcloud_positive, interpolation='bilinear')
ax1.set_title('Most Common Words in Positive Reviews (4-5 Stars)', fontsize=20)
ax1.axis('off')
ax2.imshow(wordcloud_negative, interpolation='bilinear')
ax2.set_title('Most Common Words in Negative Reviews (1-2 Stars)', fontsize=20)
ax2.axis('off')
plt.show()


# Bar chart: top 20 words in positive vs negative
# It also generates top-20 word frequency bar charts for both positive and negative reviews.
def top_words(text, n=20, stops=custom_stops):
    words = [w.lower() for w in text.split() if w.lower() not in stops and len(w) > 3]
    return Counter(words).most_common(n)

pos_words = top_words(positive_reviews)
neg_words = top_words(negative_reviews)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))
ax1.barh([w for w,_ in pos_words], [c for _,c in pos_words], color='teal')
ax1.set_title('Top 20 Positive Review Words')
ax1.invert_yaxis()
ax2.barh([w for w,_ in neg_words], [c for _,c in neg_words], color='tab:red')
ax2.set_title('Top 20 Negative Review Words')
ax2.invert_yaxis()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations:

Positive Reviews (Rating ≥ 4):

  1. Dominant words: "love", "size", "wear", "great", "perfect", "comfortable", "fabric", "color", "fits" — reflecting strong emotional satisfaction alongside attention to physical product attributes.

  2. Fit-related positivity: Words like "fits", "perfect", "flattering", "size" appear prominently, confirming that when sizing works, it is the single biggest driver of positive sentiment.

  3. Repurchase and loyalty signals: "Bought", "ordered", "wear", "love" suggest customers are returning buyers who actively use and recommend products — indicating strong brand loyalty.

  4. Material and aesthetic focus: "Fabric", "color", "soft", "comfortable", "beautiful" show that satisfied customers value both the tactile quality and visual appeal of their purchases.

Negative Reviews (Rating ≤ 2):

  1. Dominant words: "fabric", "size", "fit", "look", "material", "ordered", "back", "disappointed", "quality", "returned" — centering almost entirely around sizing failures and material disappointments.
  2. Sizing is the #1 complaint: "Size", "fit", "small", "look" dominate the word cloud and bar chart, confirming that sizing inconsistency is the primary driver of dissatisfaction — notably, "size" and "fabric" rank #1 and #2 in frequency.
  3. Return behavior is explicit: "Ordered", "back", "returned", "wanted" cluster together, showing that negative experiences directly and immediately translate to return actions — a significant operational cost.
  4. Overlap with positive vocabulary is revealing: Words like "love", "beautiful", and "fabric" appear in both positive and negative clouds — suggesting customers had high expectations going in, making the disappointment more acute when fit or quality failed to deliver.

Key Insight for the Problem: The word clouds reveal a striking asymmetry: positive reviews are driven by emotional satisfaction and confirmed fit, while negative reviews are driven by sizing inconsistency and fabric/material quality failures. Crucially, the bar charts make this quantitative — "fabric" and "size" dominate negative word frequency at nearly 500 and 450 counts respectively, while positive reviews are more evenly distributed across emotional and product terms. This means our GenAI pipeline's retail insights should consistently surface sizing standardisation and material quality audits as the highest-priority improvement areas. If the LLM's outputs frequently tag these themes in negative reviews, we can be confident it has correctly captured the dataset's core patterns.

custom_stops = STOPWORDS | {'dress','top','shirt','one','also','would','could','really','very', 'clothing'}


## 5.3 Qualitative Insights: Word Clouds for Neutral Reviews
# Separate reviews into the group based on rating:
# - Neutral:  Rating == 3 (3 star reviews — mixed or indifferent sentiment)
# We join all review texts in each group into a single long string for word cloud generation

neutral_reviews = " ".join(df[df['Rating'] == 3]['Review.Text'])

# Generate WordCloud for negative reviews
# background_color='black' with colormap='Greys' creates a muted, ambiguous tone matching 3-star sentiment
wordcloud_neutral = WordCloud(width=800, height=400, stopwords=custom_stops, background_color='black', colormap='Greys').generate(neutral_reviews)

# Plot the word clouds side-by-side using matplotlib subplots
# figsize=(20, 10) creates a large figure for readability
fig, (ax3) = plt.subplots(figsize=(20, 10))
ax3.imshow(wordcloud_neutral, interpolation='bilinear')
ax3.set_title('Most Common Words in Neutral Reviews (3 Stars)', fontsize=20)
ax3.axis('off')
plt.show()


# Bar chart: top 20 words in positive vs negative
# It also generates top-20 word frequency bar charts for neutral reviews.
def top_words(text, n=20, stops=custom_stops):
    words = [w.lower() for w in text.split() if w.lower() not in stops and len(w) > 3]
    return Counter(words).most_common(n)

neu_words = top_words(neutral_reviews)

fig, (ax3) = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 6))
ax3.barh([w for w,_ in neu_words], [c for _,c in neu_words], color='grey')
ax3.set_title('Top 20 Neutral Review Words')
ax3.invert_yaxis()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Neutral Reviews (Rating = 3):

  1. Dominant words: "fabric", "size", "fit", "look", "color", "material", "ordered", "back", "small", "quality" — a vocabulary that sits squarely between praise and complaint, reflecting customers who found things to like and dislike in equal measure.

  2. Fabric and size lead at high frequency: The bar chart shows "fabric" at ~750 and "size" at ~625 — both higher in raw count than their equivalents in the negative reviews. This tells us that 3-star customers are not silent about these issues; they are engaging with them but not decisively enough to rate low.

  3. Ambivalent emotional language: Words like "love", "beautiful", "flattering", "cute", and "great" appear alongside "return", "small", "thin", "tight", and "wanted" — capturing the defining characteristic of a 3-star review: something worked, something didn't.

  4. Fit concerns without full rejection: "Fit", "small", "size", "back", "waist", "shoulder" all appear prominently, suggesting sizing was still a problem — but unlike in negative reviews, it wasn't bad enough to fully put the customer off. The product was close, not catastrophically wrong.

  5. "Ordered" and "tried" signal hesitation: The high frequency of "ordered", "tried", "wanted", and "looked" suggests these customers went in with specific expectations that were only partially met — they did the research but the product didn't fully deliver.

Key Insight: Neutral reviews are not indifferent — they are conflicted. The word cloud reveals customers who genuinely wanted to love the product but were held back by the same issues driving negative reviews: fabric quality and sizing. This group represents the highest conversion opportunity for the business. A small improvement in size consistency or material quality could shift a large portion of 3-star reviewers into 4–5 star territory. The GenAI pipeline should flag these reviews specifically, as they carry actionable signals that are less emotionally charged and more constructively worded than 1–2 star reviews.

Section 6: Building the Generative AI Pipeline¶

We will now build a system to analyze the reviews. This involves setting up the AI client, designing prompts, generating structured data, and evaluating the results. Use gpt-4o-mini model

Setup AI Client and Data Sample¶

Questions:

  1. How do you initialize the OpenAI client with your API key and the correct base URL?
In [234]:
# --- OpenAI API Setup ---
# Fetch the stored API key from Google Colab's secure storage
# userdata.get() retrieves secrets stored in Colab's environment (set via Colab Secrets panel)
api_key = userdata.get('OPENAI_API_KEY')

# Initialize the OpenAI client with:
# - api_key: our authentication credential
# - base_url: custom proxy URL that routes requests through Great Learning's API gateway
#   (this allows budget tracking and rate limiting)
client = openai.OpenAI(
    api_key=api_key,
    base_url='https://aibe.mygreatlearning.com/openai/v1'
)

# Set the model name as a variable for easy reuse across all API calls
# gpt-4o-mini is a cost-effective model that balances performance and token cost
model_name = 'gpt-4o-mini'

Note:¶

For this project, we will analyze and categorize a sample of 50 customer reviews. This number is chosen intentionally. Since the API has a budget limit of $20, running prompts on very large datasets can quickly exhaust your quota—especially because this exercise may involve multiple iterations, prompt refinements, and repeated evaluations.

To avoid unnecessary cost and ensure efficient experimentation, we recommend the following approach:

  • Use very small samples (5–10 reviews) during the initial testing phase to validate your prompt structure and logic.

  • Scale up to 50 reviews for the final evaluation phase, ensuring you get enough data to compare prompting techniques without draining your budget.

  • This strategy helps maintain cost control while still providing meaningful insights across Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought techniques.

If your API quota gets exhausted, you may temporarily switch to another Free AI assistant API. However, note that external tools may also have rate limits or token caps, so you will need to build retry logic and manage throttling within your code.

Section 6.1: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation¶

We will test three different prompting techniques. For each, we will create a basic version (V1) and an enhanced version (V2).

Think about it: Why is it important to have a consistent and robust evaluation framework? How can we use an "LLM-as-Judge" to score the quality of our generated outputs objectively?

Technique 1: Zero-Shot Prompting¶

Questions:

  1. How would you design a basic Zero-Shot prompt that asks the model for Category, Sentiment, Summary, Personalized Message, and Retail Insight?

  2. How can you enhance this prompt with more business context (e.g., a company name, the importance of accuracy) to create a V2 prompt?

  3. How will you loop through the data sample to generate and store the structured output for both prompt versions?

  4. How will you apply the LLM-as-Judge to generate a evaluation score between 0 to 1 (decimal allowed) for the outputs and calculate the average score of Version 1 and Version 2 prompt?

How the process works:

  1. First, you create an LLM-as-a-judge function that can evaluate the quality of model outputs.

  2. Then, you run your Zero-Shot Prompt Version 1 on a sample of 100 reviews to generate predictions.

  3. You use the judge function to score each prediction and compute the average score for Version 1.

  4. Next, you repeat the same workflow with your Version 2 prompt, generate predictions, evaluate them, and calculate the average score for Version 2.

In [236]:
# This function sends a single review to the LLM with a given prompt and parses the structured response.
# Parameters:
#   review_text (str): The raw customer review text to analyze
#   prompt (str): The prompting template that instructs the LLM what output to produce
# Returns:
#   dict: A dictionary with keys: Category, Sentiment, Summary, Personalized_Message, Retail_Insight

def get_structured_output(review_text: str, prompt: str) -> dict:
    try:
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model_name,          # fill: model_name
            temperature=0.1,           # fill: 0.1 for slight creativity
            messages=[
                {'role': 'system', 'content': 'You are a helpful AI assistant.'},
                {'role': 'user', 'content': f'{prompt}\n\nReview: {review_text}'}
            ]
        )
    except Exception as e:
        return {'Summary': f'ERROR_CALL: {type(e).__name__}: {e}'}


    # Parse the LLM's response text into structured fields
    # The response is expected in "Key: Value" format, one per line
    text = resp.choices[0].message.content or ''
    lines = [ln.strip() for ln in text.strip().splitlines() if ln.strip()]
    out = {'Category': '', 'Sentiment': '', 'Summary': '',
           'Personalized_Message': '', 'Retail_Insight': ''}
    for line in lines:
        if ':' in line:
            key_raw, val = line.split(':', 1)
            key = key_raw.strip().lower()
            val = val.strip()
            if key.startswith('category'):          out['Category'] = val
            elif key.startswith('sentiment'):       out['Sentiment'] = val
            elif key.startswith('summary'):         out['Summary'] = val
            elif 'personal' in key:                 out['Personalized_Message'] = val
            elif 'insight' in key:                  out['Retail_Insight'] = val
    return out
In [237]:
# --- Prompting Strategies and Evaluation Framework ---

# Wrapper function for cleaner code in the loops below
def generate_output(review_text, prompt):
    return get_structured_output(review_text, prompt)


judge_prompt = """You are an expert evaluator for AI-generated retail feedback analysis.

You will be given an ORIGINAL customer review and a SUMMARY generated by an AI model.
Your job is to score the quality of the summary on four criteria, then calculate a
weighted total score.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
{review}

AI-GENERATED SUMMARY:
{output}

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STEP 1 — SCORE EACH CRITERION (use the scales below)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CRITERION 1 — FAITHFULNESS (score 0–10)
Does the summary accurately reflect only what the customer actually said?
No invented details. No distortion of meaning. No misrepresentation.
10 = Every claim in the summary traces directly back to the review
7–9 = Mostly faithful with one minor interpretive stretch
4–6 = Some claims go beyond what the customer said
1–3 = Significant distortion or fabrication
0 = Completely wrong or contradicts the review

CRITERION 2 — COMPLETENESS (score 0–10)
Does the summary capture ALL important aspects of the review?
Critical rule: if the review contains BOTH positive and negative language,
a summary that only reflects one side scores NO higher than 4.
10 = Captures every significant point including mixed sentiment
7–9 = Captures main points, misses one minor detail
4–6 = Captures dominant sentiment but misses secondary sentiment
1–3 = Misses the main point of the review
0 = Empty or irrelevant

CRITERION 3 — SPECIFICITY (score 0–10)
Does the summary reference specific product attributes mentioned in the review
such as fabric, colour, sizing, fit, durability, value, comfort?
Generic phrases like "the customer was satisfied" score 0–2 regardless of accuracy.
10 = Names two or more specific product attributes from the review
7–9 = Names one specific attribute clearly
4–6 = Vaguely implies a product attribute without naming it
1–3 = No product attributes mentioned, pure sentiment only
0 = Completely generic with no connection to the product

CRITERION 4 — CONCISENESS (score 0–10)
Is the summary appropriately brief and readable?
The ideal summary is 1–2 sentences that a retail manager could read in 5 seconds.
10 = Tight and clear — every word earns its place
7–9 = Mostly concise with minor redundancy
4–6 = Somewhat verbose or repeats a point unnecessarily
1–3 = Significantly too long or too short to be useful
0 = Unreadable or missing

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STEP 2 — CALCULATE WEIGHTED TOTAL
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Apply these weights:
  Faithfulness  × 0.40
  Completeness  × 0.30
  Specificity   × 0.20
  Conciseness   × 0.10

Formula:
  weighted_total = (Faithfulness × 0.40 + Completeness × 0.30 +
                    Specificity × 0.20 + Conciseness × 0.10) / 10

This converts your 0–10 scores into a final 0.0–1.0 score.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STEP 3 — RESPOND IN EXACTLY THIS FORMAT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Faithfulness: [0-10]
Completeness: [0-10]
Specificity: [0-10]
Conciseness: [0-10]
Score: [0.0-1.0]

Nothing else. No explanation. No preamble. Five lines only."""


def judge_output(review_text, output_text):
    """
    Sends review + summary to the judge and returns the weighted 0-1 score.
    Also stores the individual criterion scores for analysis.
    """
    try:
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model_name,
            temperature=0,
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": "You are a strict evaluation assistant. Return exactly the five lines requested. Nothing else."},
                {"role": "user", "content": judge_prompt.format(
                    review=review_text,
                    output=output_text
                )}
            ]
        )
        text = resp.choices[0].message.content.strip()

        # Parse the five lines
        scores = {}
        for line in text.splitlines():
            line = line.strip()
            if ':' in line:
                key, val = line.split(':', 1)
                key = key.strip().lower()
                val = val.strip()
                if key == 'faithfulness':  scores['faithfulness'] = float(val)
                elif key == 'completeness': scores['completeness'] = float(val)
                elif key == 'specificity':  scores['specificity']  = float(val)
                elif key == 'conciseness':  scores['conciseness']  = float(val)
                elif key == 'score':        scores['weighted']     = float(val)

        # Fallback: recalculate if the model did the maths wrong
        if all(k in scores for k in ['faithfulness','completeness','specificity','conciseness']):
            recalc = (
                scores['faithfulness'] * 0.40 +
                scores['completeness'] * 0.30 +
                scores['specificity']  * 0.20 +
                scores['conciseness']  * 0.10
            ) / 10
            scores['weighted'] = round(recalc, 3)

        return scores.get('weighted', None)

    except Exception:
        return None

Observations from Zero-Shot V1:
Score: 0.859 (Baseline)


    

  1. Strong baseline performance: Zero-Shot V1 achieved an average judge score (0.85–0.90 range) of our evaluation rubric. This demonstrates that gpt-4o-mini can perform retail review analysis at a high level even without examples or detailed context — relying entirely on its pre-trained knowledge of language and sentiment.
    

    2. 

  2. How the prompt was designed: The V1 prompt is intentionally minimal — it assigns the role "retail analyst," lists the five required output fields (Category, Sentiment, Summary, Personalized Message, Retail Insight), and provides brief format guidance. No examples, no company context, no detailed rules. This simplicity is deliberate: it establishes the lowest-effort baseline against which all subsequent techniques are measured.
    

    3. 

  3. What the code does: The loop iterates through all 50 reviews using tqdm for progress tracking. For each review, generate_output() calls the LLM API with the prompt + review text, and the response is parsed into a structured dictionary. The results are stored as new columns with the prefix ZS_V1_ and concatenated to df_sample.
    

    4. 

  4. Sentiment distribution: The V1 predictions show a clear split, the majority classified as Positive (consistent with the dataset's 77% positive skew), with a smaller set of Negative and Neutral predictions. This suggests the model correctly captures the overall sentiment landscape even without guidance.
    

    5. 

  5. Strengths at this stage: The model correctly identifies obvious positive reviews ("love this dress!") and obviously negative reviews ("shrinks after washing"). The summaries, while sometimes generic, capture the main point of most reviews.
    

    6. 

  6. Weaknesses observed: Some summaries lack specificity — e.g., "The customer was satisfied with the product" instead of referencing the specific attribute (fit, fabric, colour) the customer mentioned. Retail insights occasionally default to generic recommendations like "improve quality" rather than actionable, specific suggestions.
    

    7. 



Why this matters: A score of 0.859 is a strong baseline. Any V2 enhancement or alternative technique must beat this score to justify the added complexity and token cost. This score also tells us that simple prompting is already viable for production use cases where cost efficiency is prioritised over maximum quality.

Observations from Zero-Shot V2 (compared to V1):
Score: 0.874 (+0.015 improvement over V1's 0.859)


    

  1. V2 successfully outperformed V1: The context-enhanced V2 prompt achieved 0.874, a +0.015 improvement. While modest, this improvement is consistent and validates a key prompt engineering principle: adding business context and specific constraints improves output quality.
    

    2. 

  2. What changed in the V2 prompt: V2 added several enhancements over V1:
    

      

    • A company identity ("StyleHub") and a senior analyst role, this frames the model as a domain expert.
      • 

    • A mission statement ("Transform raw customer reviews into structured business intelligence"), this clarifies the purpose.
      • 

    • Explicit category options (Dresses, Tops, Bottoms, etc.), reducing miscategorisation.
      • 

    • Sentiment criteria with rating equivalents (e.g., "Positive = Rating 4-5 equivalent"), anchoring sentiment to concrete definitions.
      • 

    • Instructions to reference specific product attributes, encouraging detailed, non-generic summaries.
      • 

    • An example of a good retail insight, showing the model what "actionable" looks like.
      • 

    

    3. 

  3. Why V2 improved: The business context gives the model a clearer understanding of what "good" means in this domain. Instead of guessing what a "retail insight" should look like, the model has a concrete example to follow. The explicit sentiment criteria reduce ambiguity. A review that says "nice but too small" is more likely to be correctly classified as Neutral rather than forced into Positive or Negative.
    

    4. 

  4. Comparison to V1:
    

      

    • Summaries became more specific: V2 summaries more frequently reference the exact product attributes (fit, fabric, colour) mentioned in the review, rather than generic paraphrasing.
      • 

    • Retail insights became more actionable: V2 insights tend to name specific departments or actions (e.g., "update sizing chart for petite customers in the Dresses category") rather than vague recommendations.
      • 

    • Sentiment accuracy likely improved: The explicit criteria help the model correctly classify borderline reviews (Rating 3) as Neutral.
      • 

    

    5. 

  5. Cost consideration: V2 uses more tokens per call due to the longer prompt (~150 more tokens), but at gpt-4o-mini's pricing, the marginal cost is negligible (fractions of a cent per review).
    

    6. 



Answering the section questions:


    

  • How can you enhance with business context? By adding a company name, analyst role, mission statement, explicit output constraints, and an example of ideal output — as demonstrated in V2.
    • 

  • How do you apply the LLM-as-Judge? The judge receives both the original review and the model's output, then scores on accuracy, specificity, completeness, and actionability. Scores are averaged across all 50 reviews to produce a single comparable metric per technique.
    • 



Key takeaway: Zero-Shot V2's improvement confirms that specificity and context matter in prompt engineering. Even without examples (unlike Few-Shot), adding business context, explicit output criteria, and sentiment anchors produces measurably better results. Zero-Shot V2 (0.874) is the highest-scoring technique in this project and is the recommended choice for production bulk processing.

         two washes, which is inconsistent with the price point.
Personalized Message: We sincerely apologise for this quality issue. We'd love to
                       make this right — please contact us for a replacement.
Retail Insight: [QUALITY] Flag this SKU for quality audit. Pilling complaints at this
                price point will damage brand reputation and increase churn.

--- EXAMPLE 3: MIXED ---
Review: 'I tried these on in the store, and they are super cute but run small. i typically wear a size 25 (i'm 5' 5" and 108 lbs.) and they were too tight for me. i like the fabric and the cut; i think they'd be great one size up. (my store didn't have them.)'
Category: Dresses
Sentiment: Mixed
Summary: Customer appreciates the aesthetic design but encountered significant
         sizing issues requiring a return and reorder.
Personalized Message: Thank you for persisting with us! We're updating our size guide
                       for this style. We hope the new size is perfect.
Retail Insight: [SIZING] Update size guide for this SKU with 'size up 1 size'

=== MANDATORY RULES ===
RULE 1 - Category: Must be one of: Dresses | Tops | Bottoms | Jackets | Intimates | Accessories
RULE 2 - Sentiment: Must be one of: Positive | Negative | Neutral | Mixed
         Use Mixed when the review contains BOTH clear praise AND clear criticism.
         Use Neutral only when the tone is genuinely indifferent with no strong feeling.
RULE 3 - Summary: Exactly 2 sentences.
         Sentence 1 = what customer explicitly liked.
         Sentence 2 = what customer explicitly disliked or suggested improvement.
         If only positive: Sentence 2 = 'No significant concerns were raised.'
RULE 4 - Personalized Message: Must feel human, warm, and brand-consistent.
         Must acknowledge the specific feedback point and be empathetic. For negative reviews, include an apology.
         2-3 sentences maximum.
RULE 5 - Retail Insight: Must begin with a department tag: [SIZING] / [QUALITY] /
         [MARKETING] / [OPERATIONS] / [PRODUCT].
         Must contain a specific, measurable recommendation.
         Never write vague statements like 'improve product quality'.

=== NEW REVIEW TO ANALYSE ===
'''

Observations from Few-Shot Prompting (V1 and V2):
Scores: FS V1 = 0.827 | FS V2 = 0.757 (V2 dropped by -0.070)


    

  1. Few-Shot V1 scored 0.827, which is competitive with Zero-Shot V1 (0.859) but noticeably lower. This is somewhat surprising because Few-Shot prompting — which provides concrete examples — is generally expected to outperform Zero-Shot. The likely reason is that the V1 examples, while detailed, may have caused the model to overly mimic (Overfit) the example style rather than adapt to each unique review.
    

    2. 

  2. Few-Shot V2 dropped by -0.070 compared to V1 This is the most important finding in this section. V2 dropped by -0.084 compared to V1 — a substantial decline. This means the added rules and constraints in V2 actually hurt performance rather than helping it.
    

    3. 

  3. Why V2 performed worse — Root cause analysis:
    

      

    • Over-constraint: V2 added detailed rules on top of the examples (e.g., strict formatting requirements, department tags, specific sentence counts). This created conflicting priorities, the model tried to follow both the examples AND the rules simultaneously, and when they diverged, the output quality suffered.
      • 

    • Prompt length: V2's prompt is significantly longer than V1's. With gpt-4o-mini's context window, excessively long prompts can cause the model to lose focus on the core task, prioritising rule compliance over analytical quality.
      • 

    • Examples already provide implicit rules: The examples in V1 already demonstrate the expected format, tone, and quality level. Adding explicit rules on top of already-clear examples creates redundancy that confuses rather than clarifies.
      • 

    • Judge penalisation: The judge evaluates against the original review. If V2's stricter rules cause the model to produce outputs that are well-formatted but less accurately reflect the review's actual content, the judge correctly scores them lower.
      • 

    

    4. 

  4. Few-Shot prompt design — what worked and what didn't:
    

      

    • What worked (V1): Three well-chosen examples (positive, negative, mixed) with clear Category/Sentiment/Summary/Message/Insight fields. The examples came from realistic review scenarios and demonstrated the expected analytical depth.
      • 

    • What didn't work (V2): Adding a "RULES" section after the examples with strict constraints for each field. The model over-indexed on rule compliance at the expense of genuine analysis.
      • 

    

    5. 

  5. Comparison to Zero-Shot:
    

      

    • Zero-Shot V1 (0.859) > Few-Shot V1 (0.827): Minimal difference, but shows that good examples alone don't guarantee improvement.
      • 

    • Zero-Shot V2 (0.874) > Few-Shot V2 (0.757): Zero-Shot with context significantly outperforms Few-Shot with over-constrained rules.
      • 

    

    6. 



Answering the section questions:


    

  • How do you structure a Few-Shot prompt? Include 2-3 diverse examples (positive, negative, mixed) showing the exact output format. Each example should demonstrate analytical depth, not just formatting.
    • 

  • How can V2 add rules to reduce ambiguity? Rules should be minimal and complementary to examples — not redundant. Focus on 2-3 key guidelines rather than exhaustive constraints.
    • 

  • How does Few-Shot compare to Zero-Shot? In this experiment, Few-Shot V1 was comparable to Zero-Shot V1, but the enhanced versions diverged significantly: ZS V2 improved while FS V2 declined.
    • 



Key takeaway: More instructions ≠ better results. Few-Shot V2's decline demonstrates a critical prompt engineering lesson: examples and rules can conflict, and over-constraining the model reduces output quality. The fix is to keep rules minimal and let the examples do the heavy lifting.






















Technique 3: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting¶
Questions:


    

  1. How do you instruct the model to "think step-by-step" internally but only show the final, structured answer?
    

    2. 

  2. How can you combine the CoT instruction with more detailed reasoning from the COT V1 prompt to create a powerful CoT V2 prompt?
    

    3. 

  3. Does encouraging the model to reason first lead to a measurable improvement in the quality of the generated insights?
    

    4. 



How the process works:


    

  1. First, you create an LLM-as-a-judge function that can evaluate the quality of model outputs.
    

    2. 

  2. Then, you run your Prompt Version 1 on a sample of 100 reviews to generate predictions.
    

    3. 

  3. You use the judge function to score each prediction and compute the average score for Version 1.
    

    4. 

  4. Next, you repeat the same workflow with your Version 2 prompt, generate predictions, evaluate them, and calculate the average score for Version 2.
    

    5.

cot_prompt_v1 = '''
INTERNAL REASONING PROCESS (do not output these steps):
1. EMOTIONAL ANALYSIS: What is the customer's primary emotion?
   - Identify emotional words: 'love', 'disappointed', 'obsessed', 'terrible'
   - Determine overall sentiment polarity
2. FEATURE EXTRACTION: What specific product attributes are mentioned?
   - Fit, sizing, fabric, colour, style, durability, value-for-money
3. BUSINESS IMPACT: What does this mean for the business?
   - Is this a product issue, a sizing issue, a quality issue, or a marketing opportunity?
4. CUSTOMER RESPONSE: How should the brand respond to retain this customer?
   - Acknowledge the specific issue or praise
   - Avoid generic responses

OUTPUT ONLY THE FOLLOWING (no reasoning text):
Category: [clothing category]
Sentiment: [Positive | Negative | Neutral | Mixed]
Summary: [2 sentences based on your analysis above]
Personalized Message: [2-3 sentences responding to the customer's specific experience]
Retail Insight: [1 actionable insight with a department tag]
'''

Observations from Chain-of-Thought Prompting (V1 and V2):
Scores: CoT V1 = 0.809 | CoT V2 = 0.691 (V2 dropped by -0.118)


    

  1. CoT V1 scored below both Zero-Shot versions: CoT V1 achieved 0.809, which is below Zero-Shot V1 (0.859) and Zero-Shot V2 (0.874) but very competitive — only 0.050 points below the best-performing technique. While CoT prompting instructs the model to reason step-by-step before answering — which theoretically should improve analytical quality — the results suggest that for this specific task, the reasoning overhead did not translate into better structured outputs.
    

    2. 

  2. CoT V2 scored the lowest of all techniques (0.691): This is the lowest-ranking technique across all six variants, dropping -0.118 from V1. While still a respectable absolute score, it ranks last because the other techniques improved significantly under the weighted judge
    

    3. 

  3. Why CoT V2 failed — Root cause analysis:
    

      

    • Persona overload: V2 assigns a detailed persona ("Dr. Sarah Chen, Chief Retail Intelligence Officer with 15 years experience"). While creative, this level of role-playing can distract the model from the analytical task, causing it to generate responses that sound impressive but lack accuracy.
      • 

    • Excessively complex reasoning framework: V2 defines five detailed reasoning steps (Sentiment Decomposition, Product Feature Mapping, Business Impact Scoring, Response Calibration, Insight Formulation). This is too many steps for gpt-4o-mini to process internally while also producing clean structured output — the model likely attempted to output some reasoning steps despite being told not to, causing parsing failures and lower scores.
      • 

    • "Mixed" sentiment label: Both CoT V1 and V2 allow a "Mixed" sentiment label, which the other techniques don't use. The judge may penalise "Mixed" if the review is actually predominantly positive or negative, as it represents an indecisive classification.
      • 

    • Token budget exhaustion: The CoT V2 prompt is the longest of all six, consuming a significant portion of the model's token budget on instructions rather than leaving room for thoughtful analysis.
      • 

    

    4. 

  4. CoT V1 vs V2 comparison:
    

      

    • V1 had a simpler 4-step reasoning process (Emotional Analysis, Feature Extraction, Business Impact, Customer Response) — clear and manageable.
      • 

    • V2 expanded to 5 steps with sub-bullets under each step, plus a detailed persona — too complex for the model to handle cleanly.
      • 

    

    5. 

  5. Does CoT reasoning improve quality? Based on these results, no — not for this task and model. The LLM-as-Judge evaluation shows that:
    

      

    • Zero-Shot V2 (0.874) > Zero-Shot V1 (0.859) > FS V1 (0.827) > CoT V1 (0.809) > FS V2 (0.757) > CoT V2 (0.691)
      • 

    • The simpler the prompt, the better the performance — additional reasoning instructions created noise rather than signal.
      • 

    

    6. 

  6. Where CoT might still add value: Despite lower scores, the LLM comparison analysis (Cell 79) noted that CoT "recognized the complexity of customer emotions" and labelled ambiguous reviews as "Mixed" rather than forcing a binary choice. In a production system that values nuance detection over consistent labelling, CoT could serve as a secondary processor for flagged ambiguous reviews.
    

    7. 



Answering the section questions:


    

  • How do you instruct the model to "think step-by-step"? Define a clear reasoning framework (3-4 steps maximum), then explicitly state "OUTPUT ONLY THE FOLLOWING — do not include your reasoning."
    • 

  • Does reasoning improve quality? In this experiment, no. CoT V1 and CoT V2 both scored lower than Zero-Shot alternatives. The reasoning framework adds complexity without proportional quality gains for gpt-4o-mini.
    • 



Key takeaway: The clear pattern is that simpler, well-focused prompts outperform complex, over-engineered ones. Only Zero-Shot V2 improved over its V1 counterpart — because it added helpful context without adding conflicting constraints. Both Few-Shot V2 and CoT V2 declined because they added excessive rules and complexity.






















Section 7: Applying GenAI for Product Recommendation:¶
Now, let's use the model for a different task: predicting the Recommended IND flag.


Questions:


    

  1. How do you design a prompt that strictly asks for a binary output (1 or 0) and a brief reason?
    

    2. 

  2. What kind of function is needed to reliably parse the model's text response to extract the 1/0 flag and the Reason?
    

    3. 

  3. How do you evaluate the model's performance as a classifier using standard metrics like accuracy, confusion matrix, and classification report?
    

    4. 



How the Process Works


1. Prepare Data


Copy the dataset, store the original recommendation labels, and remove them from the model input to avoid leakage.


2. Generate Predictions


Use a strict two-line prompt to make the LLM output a binary recommendation (1/0) and a short reason based only on the review text.


3. Parse Outputs


Extract the flag and reason from the raw LLM response using regex-based parsing that handles formatting issues.


4. Build Prediction Table


Run the prompt for each review, parse the result, and store the predictions in a new DataFrame.


5. Evaluate Performance


Compare LLM predictions with true labels using accuracy, confusion matrix, and classification report.


6. Explain Mismatches


For incorrect predictions, generate a short explanation describing why the model’s decision may have differed from the human label.


















In [257]:






# --- Predicting Product Recommendations ---
# Step 1: Prepare the data
# Copy the sample DataFrame to avoid modifying the original
# Store the actual labels in a new column 'Actual_Recommended'
# Drop the original 'Recommended.IND' column to prevent the LLM from seeing it
# This simulates a real scenario where we only have the review text

# Fixed: Use 'df_sample_copy' instead of the undefined 'df_sample'
df_reco = df_sample_copy.copy()
df_reco["Actual_Recommended"] = df_reco["Recommended.IND"]
df_reco = df_reco.drop(columns=["Recommended.IND"])
print(f'Recommendation distribution: {df_reco["Actual_Recommended"].value_counts().to_dict()}')

























Recommendation distribution: {1: 40, 0: 10}





















In [258]:






# Step 2: Define the recommendation prediction prompt
# This prompt is designed to force a strict binary output format:
# - Line 1: "Recommended: 1" or "Recommended: 0"
# - Line 2: "Reason: [brief explanation]"
# The strict format ensures reliable regex parsing of the response.
recommendation_prompt = '''
TASK: Binary product recommendation prediction.

Based exclusively on the customer review below, output EXACTLY two lines:
Line 1: Recommended: [1 or 0]  (1=would recommend, 0=would not recommend)
Line 2: Reason: [One specific sentence citing evidence from the review]

DECISION RULES:
- Output 1 if: review contains words like 'love', 'perfect', 'great', 'will buy again',
               'recommend', 'obsessed', 'flattering', 'true to size'
- Output 0 if: review contains words like 'return', 'disappointed', 'poor quality',
               'doesn't fit', 'never again', 'waste of money', 'not as described'
- If ambiguous: use the RATING context in the review to decide (positive tone = 1)

DO NOT output anything else. No preamble, no explanation beyond the 2 lines.
'''





















In [259]:






# Step 3: Parse the LLM's response and generate predictions
# parse_recommendation_reply() extracts the binary flag and reason from the raw text
# using regex patterns to handle formatting variations in the LLM's output

def parse_recommendation_reply(raw_text):
    if raw_text is None: return (np.nan, "", "")
    s = str(raw_text).strip()
    # Look for "Recommended: 0" or "Recommended: 1" in the response
    m = re.search(r'Recommended\s*:\s*([01])\b', s, re.IGNORECASE)
    flag = int(m.group(1)) if m else np.nan
    # Look for "Reason: ..." in the response
    m3 = re.search(r'Reason\s*:\s*(.+)', s, re.IGNORECASE)
    reason = m3.group(1).strip() if m3 else ""
    return (flag, reason[:200], s)

# Generate predictions for all 50 reviews
llm_preds = []
for review in tqdm(df_reco["Review.Text"], desc="LLM Recommend Predictions"):
    # Ensure review is a string, handling potential np.nan values
    review_content = str(review) if pd.notna(review) else ""
    prompt = recommendation_prompt + "\n\nReview:\n" + review_content
    try:
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model_name,
            messages=[{"role":"user", "content": prompt}],
            temperature=0.0, max_tokens=60
        )
        raw = resp.choices[0].message.content or ""
    except Exception as e:
        raw = f"""ERROR: {type(e).__name__}: {e}

Review causing error: {review_content}"""

    flag, reason, raw_clean = parse_recommendation_reply(raw)
    llm_preds.append({"LLM_Recommended_Raw": raw_clean, "LLM_Recommended_Flag": flag, "LLM_Recommend_Reason": reason})

llm_pred_df = pd.DataFrame(llm_preds)
df_reco = pd.concat([df_reco.reset_index(drop=True), llm_pred_df.reset_index(drop=True)], axis=1)

























LLM Recommend Predictions: 100%|██████████| 50/50 [00:39<00:00,  1.28it/s]

# --- Evaluating Model Performance ---

    print('No valid predictions found to evaluate. This is likely due to API rate limits or errors during generation.')
else:

    y_pred = eval_df['LLM_Recommended_Flag'].astype(int)

    acc = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)

    # Only generate report if we have at least one of each class or it will still error

Observations from Product Recommendation Prediction:
Accuracy: 92.0% | 4 mismatches out of 50


    

  1. The LLM achieved 92% accuracy as a binary classifier, correctly predicting whether a customer would recommend the product for 46 out of 50 reviews. This significantly outperforms the naive majority-class baseline of 80% (since 40 out of 50 sampled reviews were Recommended=1). The LLM is not simply guessing "1" for everything — it is genuinely analysing review text to make informed predictions.
    

    2. 

  2. Confusion Matrix breakdown:
    

      

    • True Positives (Recommended=1, Predicted=1): 36 — The LLM correctly identified 36 out of 40 recommended products.
      • 

    • True Negatives (Recommended=0, Predicted=0): 10 — The LLM correctly identified all 10 non-recommended products — a perfect recall of 100% for the minority class.
      • 

    • False Negatives (Recommended=1, Predicted=0): 4 — The LLM incorrectly predicted 4 recommended products as not recommended. These are likely reviews with mixed language ("I love the design but the sizing was off") where the negative language triggered a "0" prediction despite the human recommending the product.
      • 

    • False Positives (Recommended=0, Predicted=1): 0 — The LLM never predicted "recommend" for a product the human said "do not recommend." This is excellent — the model is conservative in its positive predictions.
      • 

    

    3. 

  3. Classification Report analysis:
    

      

    • Class 0 (Not Recommended): Precision = 0.714, Recall = 1.000, F1 = 0.833. The recall of 1.000 means the model catches every single negative review — no dissatisfied customers slip through undetected. The lower precision (0.714) means some reviews predicted as "not recommended" were actually recommended — these are the 4 false negatives.
      • 

    • Class 1 (Recommended): Precision = 1.000, Recall = 0.900, F1 = 0.947. Perfect precision means every review the model flags as "recommended" truly is recommended. The 90% recall means 4 out of 40 recommended reviews were missed.
      • 

    

    4. 

  4. Business interpretation:
    

      

    • The model's perfect recall for Class 0 is highly valuable — it means every dissatisfied customer is identified, enabling proactive outreach and issue resolution.
      • 

    • The 4 false negatives are acceptable — these represent borderline reviews where the customer ultimately recommended despite expressing concerns. Flagging these for human review is actually useful for quality assurance.
      • 

    

    5. 

  5. Why 92% accuracy matters: Traditional sentiment classifiers require labelled training data and model training. This LLM achieved 92% accuracy with zero training data — just a well-designed prompt. This demonstrates the practical viability of using LLMs as zero-training classifiers for retail analytics.
    

    6. 



Answering the section questions:


    

  • How do you design a strict binary prompt? Force the output to exactly two lines: "Recommended: [1/0]" and "Reason: [one sentence]." Use temperature=0.0 for deterministic output.
    • 

  • What parsing function is needed? Regex-based parsing using re.search(r'Recommended\s*:\s*([01])\b', text) to extract the flag, handling formatting variations.
    • 

  • How do you evaluate classifier performance? Using accuracy, confusion matrix (for TP/TN/FP/FN breakdown), and classification report (precision, recall, F1 per class).
    •
